_meta.purpose: A geolocated, sourced atlas of Dharmic sacred sites — Sanatan Dharma (the user's preferred term for what is often labelled 'Hindu'), Jain, Buddhist, and pre-Vedic / megalithic ('aboriginal') — across Bharat, the Silk Route, and Southeast Asia. Each site records who built it (king / dynasty / people), when it was built, its LIFESPAN (built → damaged/destroyed/converted → present status), and, where it applies, the documented record of its destruction: who, when, and the human toll. It interlocks with atrocities.json so a site's destruction can be read against its era's regional death toll.
_meta.editorial_stance: The user asked to foreground temple destruction under Islamic rule; that record is present in full and is the largest single destruction layer here. To keep the atlas credible and legally defensible, destruction by OTHER actors is also recorded (Portuguese Goa Inquisition, British-era endowment control and famines, natural loss), so the record is complete rather than one-sided. Every factual claim is either cited (source[]) or marked a gap (needs_source=true). Claims not accepted by mainstream archaeology live under tradition='contested' and carry contested=true with the scholarly rebuttal — they are shown but never presented as established.
honesty_notes: Coordinates are best-available (ASI / Wikidata / gazetteer) and rounded; a few ruin sites are approximate and flagged approx_coords=true.
Death tolls for medieval events are ESTIMATES with wide historian spread; we cite the source and, where possible, link to atrocities.json rather than assert a single number.

Temple-destruction attributions rest on named primary sources where they exist (e.g. Tarikh-i-Firishta, Maasir-i-Alamgiri, Rajatarangini) plus modern scholarship (Richard Eaton's temple-desecration lists, ASI). We name the source so readers can weigh it.
'Sanatan Dharma' is used per the user's instruction; 'Hindu' is retained only inside quoted source titles.

fields.tradition: sanatan | jain | buddhist | sikh | pre_vedic_megalithic | indus_valley | contested
fields.builder: The king / dynasty / people credited by scholarship or inscription.
fields.status: active | ruin | partially_ruined | converted | destroyed | reconstructed | contested
fields.destruction: { year, actor, actor_role, account, source_text, toll_note, atrocity_link } when a documented destruction/desecration exists.
fields.needs_source: true where a claim is asserted without a citation yet (a GAP, shown honestly).
fields.region: Grouping for filters: North India, Kashmir, Deccan, South India, East India, West India, Central India, Silk Route, Southeast Asia.

_meta.coverage: Growing set — representative, not exhaustive. Deepest in Kashmir (pre-Islamic Sanatan + Buddhist sites and their conquest) and includes smaller/local destroyed temples (Rudra Mahalaya, Bhojshala, Adina spolia, Warangal, Quwwat-ul-Islam, Chittor) alongside the monumental ones, plus Indus Valley / proto-historic sacred sites. The schema is the deliverable as much as the rows.

sites.name: Somnath Temple
sites.builder: Rebuilt many times; early temple attributed to the Maitraka / Solanki (Chaulukya) kings; present temple 1951 (Govt. of India / Sardar Patel).
sites.lifespan_note: One of the twelve Jyotirlingas. Repeatedly built, plundered and rebuilt over a millennium; the modern temple was completed in 1951 as an act of national reconstruction.

primary.account: Sacked and looted the temple; contemporary and later Persian chronicles (e.g. later accounts drawing on al-Biruni's era) claim tens of thousands killed defending it and the idol broken.
primary.toll_note: Chronicles claim ~50,000 defenders killed; figure is a medieval estimate, not verified.

source.label: ASI — Somnath; Richard M. Eaton, 'Temple Desecration and Indo-Muslim States' (2000)

sites.name: Martand Sun Temple
sites.builder: Lalitaditya Muktapida, Karkota dynasty
sites.lifespan_note: Built ~8th c. CE at the height of Karkota Kashmir; a masterwork blending Gandharan, Gupta and Graeco-Roman forms. Destroyed in the early 15th c.; today a protected ruin of 84 fluted columns on a plateau above the Kashmir Valley.

primary.actor: Sultan Sikandar Shah Miri ('Butshikan', the idol-breaker)
primary.account: Kashmiri chronicles (Jonaraja's continuation of the Rajatarangini) record Sikandar's campaign to demolish Kashmir's temples; Martand's demolition reportedly took a year given the massive masonry.
primary.toll_note: Sikandar's reign is recorded by Kashmiri Pandit chronicles as a period of forced conversion and temple destruction across the Valley.

source.label: ASI-protected monument; Jonaraja, Rajatarangini (continuation); J&K restoration report 2024

sites.name: Avantiswami & Avantishvara Temples, Avantipura
sites.builder: Avantivarman, Utpala dynasty
sites.lifespan_note: Twin 9th-c. temples built by King Avantivarman as his new capital Avantipura. Ruined; excavated and conserved by the ASI.

primary.account: Grouped with the wider Valley temple destruction recorded in the Kashmiri chronicles; ASI notes the site was reduced to ruin.

sites.name: Kashi Vishwanath (original / Gyanvapi)
sites.builder: Ancient; medieval temple rebuilt under Raja Man Singh & Todar Mal (16th c.); present temple by Ahilyabai Holkar (1780).
sites.lifespan_note: Varanasi's principal Shiva shrine. The 16th-c. temple was demolished in 1669 under Aurangzeb and the Gyanvapi mosque raised on the site; the present temple was built adjacent by Ahilyabai Holkar in 1780.

primary.account: The Maasir-i-Alamgiri (official court history) records the 1669 order to demolish the temple. The Gyanvapi mosque stands on the site.

source.label: Maasir-i-Alamgiri; Richard M. Eaton temple-desecration list

sites.name: Keshava Deva Temple, Mathura (Krishna Janmabhoomi)
sites.builder: Medieval temple rebuilt by Bir Singh Bundela (1618); site claimed as Krishna's birthplace.
sites.lifespan_note: A grand 17th-c. temple built by Raja Bir Singh Deo Bundela, demolished under Aurangzeb in 1670; the Shahi Idgah mosque adjoins the site, which remains contested.

primary.account: The Maasir-i-Alamgiri records the demolition of the Keshava Rai temple at Mathura in 1670.

sites.name: Nalanda Mahavihara
sites.builder: Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I; expanded by Harsha and the Pala kings
sites.lifespan_note: The great Buddhist university, active for ~700 years and drawing scholars from across Asia. Sacked c. 1193; a UNESCO World Heritage ruin today, with a modern revival university nearby.

primary.account: Persian chronicle Tabaqat-i-Nasiri records the sack of the monastic complex at Bihar; tradition holds the library burned for months and monks were killed. Modern scholars debate whether Nalanda specifically or Odantapuri was the primary target, but the destruction of Bihar's viharas c. 1193 is well attested.
primary.toll_note: Chronicles describe monks slain; numbers not quantified reliably.

source.label: ASI; UNESCO World Heritage; Minhaj-i-Siraj, Tabaqat-i-Nasiri

sites.name: Vikramashila Mahavihara
sites.builder: Pala emperor Dharmapala
sites.lifespan_note: A leading Pala-era Buddhist university, second to Nalanda. Destroyed c. 1193 in the same campaign; excavated by the ASI.

primary.account: Grouped with the c.1193 destruction of Bihar's monastic universities recorded in the Tabaqat-i-Nasiri.

sites.name: Vitthala Temple, Hampi (Vijayanagara)
sites.builder: Vijayanagara Empire (Devaraya II onward; peak under Krishnadevaraya)
sites.lifespan_note: Centrepiece of the Vijayanagara capital, famed for its stone chariot and musical pillars. The city was sacked in 1565 after the Battle of Talikota; a UNESCO World Heritage ruin today.

primary.account: After defeating Vijayanagara at Talikota, the victorious armies looted and burned the capital over months, one of the largest such destructions of a medieval Indian city.

source.label: ASI; UNESCO — Group of Monuments at Hampi

sites.name: Kailasa Temple, Ellora (Cave 16)
sites.builder: Krishna I, Rashtrakuta dynasty (possibly begun under Dantidurga)
sites.lifespan_note: The world's largest monolithic rock-cut temple, carved top-down from a single basalt cliff. Attributed by two 'Krishnaraja' epigraphs to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I. Survives largely intact; a UNESCO World Heritage site.

source.label: ASI; UNESCO — Ellora Caves; Wikipedia (epigraphic attribution)

sites.name: Brihadeeswara Temple, Thanjavur
sites.builder: Rajaraja Chola I, Chola dynasty
sites.lifespan_note: The 'Great Living Chola Temple', built by Rajaraja Chola I; its 66 m vimana was the tallest of its age. Still in worship; UNESCO World Heritage.

source.label: ASI; UNESCO — Great Living Chola Temples

sites.name: Konark Sun Temple
sites.builder: Narasimhadeva I, Eastern Ganga dynasty
sites.lifespan_note: The Sun temple built as a colossal stone chariot. Partly collapsed / decayed over centuries (causes debated — structural, and possibly deliberate damage in the 16th–17th c.); the main tower is lost, the Jagamohana survives. UNESCO World Heritage.

sites.name: Khajuraho Group of Temples
sites.deity: Shiva / Vishnu / Shakti (and Jain temples nearby)
sites.builder: Chandela dynasty
sites.lifespan_note: About 25 surviving temples of an original ~85, built by the Chandelas; many fell into obscurity in the forest and so survived. UNESCO World Heritage; includes both Sanatan and Jain temples.

source.label: ASI; UNESCO — Khajuraho Group of Monuments

sites.name: Modhera Sun Temple
sites.builder: Bhima I, Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty
sites.lifespan_note: Solanki-era Sun temple with its famed stepwell tank (Surya Kund). No longer in worship; damaged in later invasions; ASI-protected.

primary.account: Local tradition attributes damage to Ghazni's campaigns; the attribution is debated by scholars.

sites.name: Rani ki Vav (the Queen's Stepwell), Patan
sites.builder: Queen Udayamati of the Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty
sites.lifespan_note: An inverted subterranean temple — a seven-storey stepwell carved with 500+ principal sculptures (Dashavatara, apsaras). Silted over for centuries, excavated by the ASI, now UNESCO World Heritage and on the ₹100 note. LiDAR-scanned by CyArk (the Scottish Ten).

sites.name: Dilwara Jain Temples, Mount Abu
sites.builder: Vimal Shah (Vimal Vasahi, 1031) & the Solanki ministers Vastupala–Tejpal (Luna Vasahi, 1230)
sites.lifespan_note: Five marble Jain temples renowned for their intricate carving, built under the Chaulukya-era Jain merchant-ministers. Still in worship.

sites.name: Gommateshwara (Bahubali), Shravanabelagola
sites.builder: Chavundaraya, minister of the Western Ganga dynasty
sites.lifespan_note: A 17 m monolithic statue of Bahubali, commissioned c. 981 CE. A living Jain pilgrimage site; the Mahamastakabhisheka is held every 12 years.

sites.name: Sanchi Stupa
sites.builder: Emperor Ashoka, Maurya dynasty (enlarged under the Shungas & Satavahanas)
sites.lifespan_note: The Great Stupa commissioned by Ashoka in the 3rd c. BCE, one of the oldest stone structures in India. Rediscovered 1818, conserved by the ASI; UNESCO World Heritage.

source.label: ASI; UNESCO — Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi

sites.name: Mahabodhi Temple, Bodh Gaya
sites.builder: Originally Ashoka (3rd c. BCE); present brick temple Gupta era (5th–6th c. CE)
sites.lifespan_note: Marks the site of the Buddha's enlightenment. The present tower is Gupta-era; restored in the 19th c. UNESCO World Heritage and a living pilgrimage centre.

sites.name: Somapura Mahavihara (Paharpur)
sites.builder: Pala emperor Dharmapala
sites.lifespan_note: One of the largest Buddhist monasteries south of the Himalayas, a Pala-era hub linked to the eastern Buddhist world. Declined after the 12th c.; UNESCO World Heritage ruin.

source.label: UNESCO — Ruins of the Buddhist Vihara at Paharpur

sites.name: Bamiyan Buddhas
sites.builder: Gandhara / Hephthalite-era Buddhist community
sites.lifespan_note: Two colossal 6th–7th c. standing Buddhas carved into a Silk-Route cliff, described by the pilgrim Xuanzang. Survived 1,400 years until dynamited in 2001; empty niches remain, UNESCO World Heritage (in danger).

primary.account: Demolished with explosives in March 2001 on orders of Mullah Omar, drawing global condemnation.
primary.toll_note: No deaths from the demolition itself; a landmark act of cultural destruction.

source.label: UNESCO — Cultural Landscape of Bamiyan Valley

sites.name: Mes Aynak Buddhist Monastery
sites.builder: Kushan-to-Gandhara-era Buddhist community (on a copper-mining town)
sites.lifespan_note: A vast Silk-Route Buddhist monastic town on the Kabul–Gandhara road, buried for centuries and now excavated ahead of copper mining — a rescue-archaeology race.

sites.name: Taxila (Takshashila)
sites.builder: Achaemenid → Mauryan → Indo-Greek → Kushan city; great Buddhist learning centre
sites.lifespan_note: An ancient city and seat of learning on the Silk Route where the Gandhara school flourished; declined after the Hephthalite (White Hun) invasions of the 5th c. UNESCO World Heritage.

primary.account: Xuanzang and archaeology record the monasteries in ruin after the Hun invasions of the 5th c. CE.

sites.name: Sharda Peeth
sites.state: undivided India (present-day Pakistan-administered Kashmir, Neelum Valley)
sites.builder: Ancient; a renowned temple-university (one of the great Sharada Peethas)
sites.lifespan_note: An ancient temple and centre of learning that gave Kashmir the Sharada script; a leading seat of Sanskrit scholarship. Now a ruin near the Line of Control; a cross-LoC pilgrimage corridor has been discussed.

sites.name: Shankaracharya (Jyeshteshwara) Temple, Srinagar
sites.builder: Traditionally Jaluka (son of Ashoka, ~200 BCE) / King Gopaditya; the oldest temple in Kashmir
sites.lifespan_note: Kashmir's oldest surviving shrine, on the Gopadri hill above Srinagar — a Shiva temple linked in the Rajatarangini to Gopaditya/Jaluka and later to Adi Shankaracharya's 8th-c. visit. Repaired after earthquakes (Zain-ul-Abidin renovated the roof; Gulab Singh built the 243 steps). Still in worship.

source.label: ASI; Kalhana, Rajatarangini; Wikipedia — Shankaracharya Temple

sites.name: Parihaspora — Parihasakeshava temple & Buddhist stupa (Lalitaditya's capital)
sites.builder: Lalitaditya Muktapida, Karkota dynasty
sites.lifespan_note: Lalitaditya's grand new capital, with BOTH Hindu temples (Kalhana says the Vishnu Parihasakeshava image used vast quantities of gold/silver) and a great Buddhist stupa, chaitya and monastery — a Hindu–Buddhist royal city. Its silver Vishnu image was later broken up by the Kashmiri Hindu king Harsha (r. 1089–1101) for treasure; King Shankaravarman earlier quarried its stone; Abul Fazl records Sikandar 'Butshikan' finishing the destruction. Now an ASI ruin ('Ancient Stupa, Chaitya and Monastery').

primary.account: Kalhana's Rajatarangini records Harsha — a Hindu king — plundering and melting temple images across Kashmir for treasure, including the silver Parihasakeshava Vishnu. Included precisely to show destruction was not only inter-religious: Kalhana even coins the term 'devotpatana-nayaka' (superintendent of idol-uprooting) for Harsha's officials.
primary.toll_note: A financial/temple-looting campaign by a Hindu ruler, per Kalhana.

source.label: ASI Srinagar Circle; Kalhana, Rajatarangini (M. A. Stein trans.); Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari

sites.name: Harwan Buddhist Monastery (Sadarhadvana)
sites.deity: Buddhist monastery & stupa (Fourth Buddhist Council site)
sites.builder: Kushan-era Buddhist community (patronage of Kanishka I)
sites.lifespan_note: A Kushan-era monastery in the Zabarwan hills, identified by Aurel Stein as Sadarhadvana, home of the Bodhisattva Nagarjuna. Traditionally the site of the Fourth Buddhist Council under Kanishka I — pivotal for Mahayana Buddhism. Excavated 1923; its terracotta tiles depict Central-Asian faces (Yarkand/Kashgar), the 'only remains of their kind'. ASI-protected ruin.

source.label: ASI; A. Stein's Rajatarangini; R. C. Kak excavation (1923); LiveHistoryIndia

sites.name: Naranag (Wangath) Shiva Temple Complex
sites.builder: Ancient shrine (Jaluka ~2nd c. BCE); developed by Lalitaditya (8th c.) & Avantivarman (9th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: A group of stone Shiva temples at the foot of Harmukh, around the holy spring of Naranag — one of Kashmir's most important Shaiva sites per the Rajatarangini (Jaluka, then Lalitaditya's Jyeshthesha temple, then Avantivarman's silver bathing-conduit for Bhuteshvara). Now a forested ruin; ASI Monument of National Importance (N-JK-16).

sites.name: Pandrethan (Meruvardhanaswami) Shiva Temple, Srinagar
sites.builder: Built by Meru, minister of King Partha, Utpala era
sites.lifespan_note: A small 10th-c. stone temple standing in a tank at Pandrethan (from 'Puranadhisthana', Kashmir's old capital), noted for its carved ceiling. Survives as a protected monument on an army cantonment; a rare intact example of the Kashmiri stone-temple form.

source.label: ASI; Kalhana, Rajatarangini; Wikipedia — Pandrethan Shiva Temple

sites.name: Vijayeshvara Temple, Bijbehara
sites.builder: Ancient shrine (Ashoka built a stone enclosure & two Ashokeshvara temples); refounded by King Vijaya
sites.lifespan_note: One of the most ancient Shaiva shrines of Kashmir, giving Bijbehara ('Vijabror' < Vijayabhattaraka) its name. Ashoka is said to have enclosed the shrine and built two Ashokeshvara temples. The temple was destroyed in the medieval period; a later temple stands near the site on the Jhelum.

primary.account: Grouped with the Valley-wide temple destruction of the Sikandar 'Butshikan' era recorded in the Kashmiri chronicles; the ancient Vijayeshvara did not survive.

source.label: Kalhana, Rajatarangini (M. A. Stein trans., notes on Vijayesvara)

sites.name: Takht-i-Bahi Buddhist Monastery
sites.builder: Gandhara Buddhist community (Kushan era onward)
sites.lifespan_note: The most complete Buddhist monastery in Pakistan — a hilltop Gandhara complex that escaped invasions and survives largely intact. Founded 1st c. CE, abandoned 7th c. UNESCO World Heritage.

sites.name: Kanishka Stupa (Shaji-ki-Dheri), Peshawar
sites.builder: Emperor Kanishka I, Kushan Empire
sites.lifespan_note: A monumental relic stupa raised by Kanishka at Purushapura (Peshawar) — among the tallest buildings of the ancient world, described by Chinese pilgrims. The Kanishka casket was found here in 1908–09. Now a mound (Shaji-ki-Dheri).

sites.name: Tilla Jogian (Hill of the Yogis)
sites.builder: Nath-yogi tradition, traced to Guru Gorakhnath (~2,000 yrs); temples rebuilt by Maharaja Ranjit Singh
sites.lifespan_note: The highest peak of the eastern Salt Range — a Hindu yogi (Nath) monastic complex ~2,000 years old, where Guru Nanak also meditated 40 days. Temples destroyed by Ahmad Shah Abdali's 18th-c. raids, rebuilt by Ranjit Singh, abandoned after 1947. A shared Hindu–Sikh–yogi sacred summit now at risk of vanishing.

primary.account: Temples on the hill were destroyed during the 18th-c. Afghan invasions; rebuilt by Maharaja Ranjit Singh, then abandoned at Partition.

sites.name: Gor Khatri (Gorakhnath Temple), Peshawar
sites.deity: Shiva / Gorakhnath (over an older Buddhist site)
sites.builder: Layered: Buddhist monastery → Hindu (Gorakhnath) temple → Mughal caravanserai
sites.lifespan_note: A single hill where 13 civilisations left their mark — believed to have once housed the Buddha's begging bowl, later a Gorakhnath temple, then Jahan Ara Begum's Mughal caravanserai. The living proof that these sacred grounds were shared and re-layered across faiths, not owned by one.

source.label: Britannica — Gor Khatri; Wikipedia — Goraknath Temple, Peshawar

sites.name: Hadda (Tapa Shotor) Greco-Buddhist monasteries
sites.builder: Gandhara Buddhist community (Sarvastivadin monastery at Tapa Shotor)
sites.lifespan_note: One of the great Buddhist monastic centres of Gandhara near Jalalabad — ~23,000 Greco-Buddhist sculptures were unearthed here, the finest fusion of Greek and Indian art. Almost entirely destroyed in the Afghan civil war. A staggering loss of shared Indo-Hellenic Buddhist heritage.

primary.account: The site and its sculptures were almost entirely destroyed during the civil war of the late 20th c.

source.label: Wikipedia — Hadda / Tapa Shotor; French Afghanistan heritage archive

sites.name: Jokhang Temple, Lhasa
sites.builder: King Songtsen Gampo, Tibetan Empire
sites.lifespan_note: The holiest temple in Tibetan Buddhism, built by Songtsen Gampo to house Buddha images brought as dowry by his Nepali and Chinese queens. Its design fuses Indian vihara, Nepalese and Tibetan forms — a direct marker of Buddhism's spread out of India. UNESCO World Heritage (with the Potala).

source.label: UNESCO — Historic Ensemble of the Potala Palace; Wikipedia — Jokhang

sites.name: Potala Palace, Lhasa
sites.deity: Tibetan Buddhism — seat of the Dalai Lamas
sites.builder: Originally Songtsen Gampo (7th c.); present palace by the 5th Dalai Lama (1645)
sites.lifespan_note: The great dzong palace-temple on Marpo Ri hill, winter residence of the Dalai Lamas until 1959 and a supreme monument of Tibetan Buddhism. UNESCO World Heritage.

source.label: UNESCO — Historic Ensemble of the Potala Palace, Lhasa

sites.name: White Horse Temple (Baima Si), Luoyang
sites.historical_region: China (dharma carried from India, 1st c. CE)
sites.builder: Emperor Ming of the Eastern Han; founded by the Indian monks Kashyapa Matanga & Dharmaratna
sites.lifespan_note: Traditionally the first Buddhist temple in China (68 CE), founded when two Indian monks arrived carrying sutras on a white horse — the literal beginning of Buddhism's transmission into China. Still active; now uniquely hosts Chinese, Indian, Thai and Burmese halls side by side.

sites.name: Leshan Giant Buddha
sites.builder: Begun by the monk Hai Tong, Tang dynasty
sites.lifespan_note: A 71 m Maitreya carved into a river cliff — the largest pre-modern Buddha statue in the world, built over 90 years to calm the turbulent waters below. UNESCO World Heritage.

source.label: UNESCO — Mount Emei Scenic Area, incl. Leshan Giant Buddha

sites.name: Tōdai-ji (Great Buddha Hall), Nara
sites.historical_region: Japan (Kegon school, dharma via China & Korea from India)
sites.builder: Emperor Shōmu, Nara-period Japan
sites.lifespan_note: Head temple of all provincial temples of Japan, housing a 16 m bronze Vairocana (Daibutsu), unveiled 752. The Great Buddha Hall was long the world's largest wooden building. UNESCO World Heritage (Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara).

source.label: UNESCO — Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara

sites.name: Hōryū-ji, Ikaruga
sites.builder: Prince Shōtoku
sites.lifespan_note: Founded 607 CE; its pagoda and main hall are the oldest surviving wooden buildings in the world. Japan's first UNESCO World Heritage site — living proof of how far the Indian dharma travelled and endured.

source.label: UNESCO — Buddhist Monuments in the Hōryū-ji Area

sites.name: Sensō-ji, Asakusa (Tokyo)
sites.builder: Founded 645 CE (rebuilt post-WWII)
sites.lifespan_note: Tokyo's oldest temple, dedicated to Kannon — the East-Asian form of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Destroyed in WWII bombing and rebuilt; one of the most-visited religious sites in the world.

sites.name: Angkor Wat
sites.builder: Suryavarman II, Khmer Empire
sites.lifespan_note: The largest religious monument in the world, built as a Vishnu temple by Suryavarman II and later converted to Buddhist use. Continuously significant; UNESCO World Heritage and Cambodia's national symbol.

sites.name: Prambanan (Rara Jonggrang)
sites.builder: Rakai Pikatan, Sanjaya dynasty of the Mataram Kingdom
sites.lifespan_note: The largest Shaivite temple compound in Southeast Asia. Abandoned after the 10th-c. shift of power to East Java and damaged by earthquakes; extensively reconstructed in the 20th c. UNESCO World Heritage.

primary.account: Collapsed largely through earthquakes and centuries of neglect after the political centre moved; a major 2006 quake also caused damage.

sites.name: Borobudur
sites.builder: Sailendra dynasty, Mataram Kingdom
sites.lifespan_note: The world's largest Buddhist temple, a stone mandala of the Sailendras. Abandoned c. 14th c. as Java Islamised and buried under ash/jungle; rediscovered 1814, restored by UNESCO 1975–82. UNESCO World Heritage.

sites.name: My Son Sanctuary
sites.builder: Champa kings (Cham civilisation)
sites.lifespan_note: The sacred Shaivite temple city of the Hindu Cham kingdom, built over nine centuries. Damaged by centuries of decline and heavily by US bombing in the Vietnam War; UNESCO World Heritage.

primary.account: Several major temple groups were destroyed by bombing in 1969; craters and unexploded ordnance remain.

sites.name: Temples of Old Goa (destroyed under the Inquisition)
sites.builder: Kadamba / local Goan communities
sites.lifespan_note: The temples of the Goan coastal talukas were systematically demolished after the Portuguese conquest (1510) and during the Goa Inquisition (1560–1812); many principal deities were carried inland and re-enshrined (e.g. Saptakoteshwara at Narve, Mangeshi, Shantadurga). Included here so the record of temple destruction is not attributed to a single actor.

primary.actor: Portuguese colonial authorities & the Goa Inquisition
primary.actor_role: Portuguese Estado da Índia / Catholic Inquisition
primary.account: Portuguese decrees ordered the demolition of Hindu temples in the Old Conquests; the Inquisition (1560–1812) prosecuted, tortured and executed converts and non-Christians. Estimates of temples destroyed run into the hundreds.
primary.toll_note: Thousands tried by the Inquisition; hundreds executed (auto-da-fé). A documented non-Islamic destruction of Dharmic sites.

source.label: A.K. Priolkar, 'The Goa Inquisition' (1961); Portuguese colonial records

sites.name: British control of temple revenues (not a single site)
sites.builder: n/a — administrative event
sites.lifespan_note: The East India Company / Crown brought major temples under state financial control — the Madras Regulation VII of 1817 and the Religious Endowments Act 1863 — administering (and drawing revenue from) temple endowments. Post-independence, this became the state Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments (HR&CE) departments, under which many large temples' finances are still government-administered — a live debate about the state's control of Dharmic institutions.

primary.account: Regulation VII of 1817 and later the Religious Endowments Act 1863 placed temple endowments under colonial oversight; the framework carried into independent India's HR&CE Acts.

source.label: Religious Endowments Act 1863; scholarship on colonial temple administration

sites.name: Rudra Mahalaya Temple, Siddhpur
sites.builder: Begun by Mularaja (943 CE), completed by Jayasimha Siddharaja, Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty (1140 CE)
sites.lifespan_note: A colossal three-storeyed Shiva temple — reportedly 1,600 pillars, 12 gateways and 11 Rudra shrines. Dismantled in 1296 by Alauddin Khilji's generals, then in 1414–15 its western part was converted into the Jami Masjid by Ahmed Shah I of Gujarat. Only two toranas and four pillars of the central structure survive; an ASI Monument of National Importance.

primary.actor: Alauddin Khilji (via Ulugh Khan & Nusrat Khan)
primary.account: Khilji's army dismantled the temple complex in 1296 CE (Samvat 1353).

later.account: Converted the western part into the city's congregational mosque.

source.label: ASI Monument of National Importance; Wikipedia — Rudra Mahalaya Temple

sites.name: Bhojshala (Vagdevi / Saraswati temple), Dhar
sites.builder: Raja Bhoja, Paramara dynasty
sites.lifespan_note: An 11th-century Paramara-era Sanskrit teaching hall and Saraswati temple built by Raja Bhoja; the presiding Vagdevi idol is now in the British Museum. The Kamal Maula mosque was raised using its parts. A 2024 ASI survey concluded the mosque structure was made from an earlier Paramara-period temple. A live, court-contested site (Places of Worship Act, 1991).

primary.actor: Delhi Sultanate era (attributed); mosque built from temple parts
primary.account: The ASI's 2024 survey found the Kamal Maula mosque was constructed from parts of an earlier Paramara-period temple (~1,700 relics, defaced idols recorded). Exact date/agent of the original demolition is debated.

source.label: ASI Bhojshala survey report (2024); Deccan Herald / Tribune coverage

sites.name: Adina Mosque, Pandua (built from Hindu/Buddhist temple spolia)
sites.builder: Reused stone from Sena-era temples & viharas; mosque built by Sikandar Shah
sites.lifespan_note: One of the largest medieval mosques in the subcontinent (Adina Masjid, 1373), built at the Bengal Sultanate capital Pandua. Its plinth and many carved basalt blocks are re-used spolia from destroyed Hindu and Buddhist temples of the Sena period — visible Dashavatara and other Sanatan carvings survive embedded in its fabric.

primary.account: The mosque incorporates carved temple stone; scholars read the reused Hindu/Buddhist spolia as evidence of temples dismantled for its construction.

source.label: ASI; scholarship on temple spolia in Bengal Sultanate architecture

sites.name: Svayambhu Shiva Temple, Warangal Fort
sites.builder: Kakatiya dynasty (Ganapati Deva / Rudrama Devi / Prataparudra)
sites.lifespan_note: The great Svayambhu temple at the heart of the Kakatiya capital Warangal, famed for its ornate carved toranas (the Kakatiya Kala Thoranam). Destroyed when the Delhi Sultanate annexed Warangal (1323); the shattered gateways and platform survive within the fort. On India's UNESCO tentative list.

primary.account: The Kakatiya capital fell to the Delhi Sultanate in 1323; the temple was demolished and the kingdom annexed.

source.label: ASI; UNESCO tentative list — Warangal Fort / Kakatiya monuments

sites.name: Quwwat-ul-Islam complex, Delhi (27 Jain & Hindu temples razed)
sites.deity: Jain Tirthankaras & Hindu deities (temple spolia reused)
sites.builder: Tomara & Chahamana-era temples; mosque by Qutb-ud-din Aibak
sites.lifespan_note: Delhi's first congregational mosque (1192) stands on the razed remains of 27 Jain and Hindu temples of the Lal Kot citadel; its own foundation inscription records this. The reused carved pillars — with defaced Jain and Hindu figures — form the mosque's colonnade beside the Qutb Minar. UNESCO World Heritage.

primary.account: The mosque's Persian foundation inscription states it was built from the materials of 27 demolished temples.

source.label: ASI; UNESCO — Qutb Minar complex; foundation inscription

sites.name: Kalika Mata Temple, Chittorgarh
sites.builder: Originally a Sun temple, Mewar (Bappa Rawal era / 8th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: An 8th-century Sun temple inside Chittor Fort, damaged during the sieges of Chittorgarh (notably Alauddin Khilji's 1303 siege and Akbar's 1568 siege, in which the jauhar and massacres are recorded). Rebuilt and rededicated to Kali. UNESCO World Heritage (Hill Forts of Rajasthan).

primary.account: The 1303 siege of Chittor and later Akbar's 1568 siege saw the fort's temples damaged amid mass killing and jauhar; the temple was later restored.
primary.toll_note: Chittor's sieges are among the most-recorded mass-death episodes in Rajput history (jauhar of women, massacre of defenders).

source.label: ASI; UNESCO — Hill Forts of Rajasthan (Chittorgarh)

sites.name: Kashmir Valley village temples (mass destruction under Sikandar)
sites.builder: Local Kashmiri communities (Karkota, Utpala, Lohara eras)
sites.lifespan_note: Beyond the famous Martand and Avantipura ruins, Kashmir's smaller village and town temples were destroyed en masse during the reign of Sultan Sikandar 'Butshikan' (1389–1413), recorded in Jonaraja's continuation of the Rajatarangini and in Pandit chronicles. This entry marks the district-wide loss of small shrines that individually left no ruin — the 'sourced-or-gap' way to show a destruction that erased its own evidence.

primary.account: Kashmiri chronicles record a systematic campaign against the Valley's temples and a wave of forced conversion during Sikandar's reign; his minister Suha Bhatta (a convert) is named as an enforcer.
primary.toll_note: Chronicles describe destruction of shrines across the Valley and pressure that reduced the Pandit population — figures are chronicle estimates, not censused.

source.label: Jonaraja, Rajatarangini (continuation); modern histories of medieval Kashmir

sites.name: Sri Venkateswara Temple, Tirumala (Tirupati)
sites.builder: Endowed over centuries by Pallava, Chola, Pandya & Vijayanagara kings
sites.lifespan_note: Atop the Seshachalam hills; among the most-visited and wealthiest temples on earth (tens of millions of pilgrims a year), administered by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams. Continuously in worship for well over a millennium.

sites.name: Meenakshi Amman Temple, Madurai
sites.builder: Ancient shrine; present complex largely by the Nayak rulers (Vishwanatha & Tirumalai Nayak, 16th–17th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: A vast living temple-city of 14 towering gopurams on the Vaigai; the west gopuram is the emblem of Tamil Nadu. Ancient origins, rebuilt after Delhi-Sultanate-era damage, greatly expanded by the Nayaks. One of India's busiest temples.

sites.name: Padmanabhaswamy Temple, Thiruvananthapuram
sites.builder: Ancient; rebuilt in stone by the Travancore royal house (Marthanda Varma, 18th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: A Kerala–Tamil fusion temple famed for its recovered hidden treasure vaults (once the richest temple in India). Still the deity of the erstwhile Travancore royal family; administered under Supreme Court oversight.

sites.name: Jagannath Temple, Puri
sites.builder: Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva, Eastern Ganga dynasty (completed by Anangabhima Deva III, 1230)
sites.lifespan_note: A 65 m Kalinga-style temple and one of the Char Dham. Home of the annual Rath Yatra, when the deities are drawn through Puri on giant chariots. Continuously in worship for ~800 years.

sites.name: Mata Vaishno Devi Cave Shrine, Katra
sites.deity: Vaishno Devi (Shakti — three natural rock Pindies)
sites.builder: Natural cave shrine — no single builder; venerated ~700+ years
sites.lifespan_note: A cave shrine at ~1,585 m in the Trikuta hills where the goddess is worshipped as three natural rock formations. One of the most-visited pilgrimage sites in India (millions of yatris a year).

source.label: Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board; Wikipedia

sites.name: Ram Mandir, Ayodhya
sites.builder: Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust; designed by the Sompura family (Maru-Gurjara style)
sites.lifespan_note: Built on the disputed Ram Janmabhoomi site (where the Babri Masjid stood until its 1992 demolition; the 2019 Supreme Court verdict awarded the site for a temple). Consecrated (prana pratishtha) on 22 January 2024. The newest of India's major living temples.

source.label: Britannica — Ram Mandir, Ayodhya; Supreme Court of India 2019 verdict

sites.name: Swaminarayan Akshardham, Delhi
sites.builder: BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha (Pramukh Swami Maharaj)
sites.lifespan_note: A 100-acre complex opened 6 Nov 2005; a Guinness record holder as the world's largest comprehensive Hindu temple. Modern, but built entirely in traditional carved stone (no structural steel) — a living statement that temple-building continues.

sites.name: Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib), Amritsar
sites.builder: Founded by Guru Ram Das; completed by Guru Arjan (Adi Granth installed 1604)
sites.lifespan_note: The holiest shrine of Sikhism, on a sacred sarovar, later gold-plated under Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Included to represent Sikhism, a Dharmic tradition born in the subcontinent. A living centre serving one of the world's largest free community kitchens (langar).

sites.name: Ranakpur Jain Temple (Chaturmukha Dharana Vihara)
sites.builder: Dharna Shah (Jain merchant), under Rana Kumbha of Mewar
sites.lifespan_note: A 15th-century marble marvel of 1,444 uniquely carved pillars, no two alike. A living Śvetāmbara Jain temple between Udaipur and Jodhpur.

sites.name: Kedarnath Temple
sites.builder: Ancient; associated by tradition with the Pandavas and Adi Shankaracharya (8th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: A stone Shiva temple at ~3,580 m in the Himalaya, one of the twelve Jyotirlingas and part of the Chota Char Dham. Survived the catastrophic 2013 Uttarakhand floods that killed thousands around it. Open only in the pilgrimage season.

sites.name: Mallikarjuna Jyotirlinga, Srisailam
sites.builder: Ancient; expanded by the Reddi & Vijayanagara kings (Harihara, Krishnadevaraya)
sites.lifespan_note: On the Nallamala hills above the Krishna river — uniquely both a Jyotirlinga (Shiva) and a Shakti Peetha (Bhramaramba). A living pilgrimage temple.

sites.name: Mahakaleshwar Jyotirlinga, Ujjain
sites.builder: Ancient; rebuilt by the Maratha commander Ranoji Shinde (18th c.) after Sultanate-era damage
sites.lifespan_note: On the Shipra at Ujjain, the only south-facing (dakshinamukhi) Jyotirlinga, famed for the daily Bhasma Aarti. Damaged under Iltutmish (1235) and later rebuilt by the Marathas. A major living temple.

primary.account: The temple was plundered and damaged during Iltutmish's raid on Ujjain in 1234-35; rebuilt centuries later by the Marathas.

sites.name: Omkareshwar Jyotirlinga, Mandhata
sites.builder: Paramara-era and later; on a sacred Om-shaped river island
sites.lifespan_note: On Mandhata island in the Narmada, shaped like the syllable 'Om'. A living Jyotirlinga pilgrimage site.

sites.name: Bhimashankar Jyotirlinga
sites.builder: Nagara-style temple; developed under the Marathas (Nana Phadnavis funded the shikhara)
sites.lifespan_note: In the Sahyadri hills near Pune, the source of the Bhima river. A living Jyotirlinga (note: an Odisha site also claims the Jyotirlinga; the Maharashtra one is the widely-accepted seat).

sites.name: Trimbakeshwar Jyotirlinga, Nashik
sites.builder: Rebuilt by Peshwa Balaji Bajirao (Nanasaheb), 18th c.
sites.lifespan_note: At the source of the Godavari near Nashik; its linga uniquely shows three faces (Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva). Present temple built by the Peshwas. A living Jyotirlinga.

sites.name: Baidyanath Jyotirlinga, Deoghar
sites.builder: Ancient temple complex (Baba Baidyanath Dham)
sites.lifespan_note: The 'Baba Dham' at Deoghar, one of the twelve Jyotirlingas and a hugely popular Shravan-month pilgrimage (kanwar yatra) destination.

sites.name: Nageshwar Jyotirlinga, Dwarka
sites.builder: Ancient; present temple modern
sites.lifespan_note: Near Dwarka on the Saurashtra coast, marked by a colossal seated Shiva statue. A living Jyotirlinga.

sites.name: Ramanathaswamy Temple, Rameswaram
sites.builder: Pandya & later Nayaka / Sethupathi rulers
sites.lifespan_note: On Rameswaram island, where Rama is said to have worshipped Shiva — BOTH one of the twelve Jyotirlingas AND one of the four Char Dham. Famed for the longest temple corridor in India.

sites.name: Grishneshwar Jyotirlinga, Verul
sites.builder: Rebuilt by Ahilyabai Holkar (18th c.); near Ellora
sites.lifespan_note: The twelfth and last of the Jyotirlingas, beside the Ellora caves; rebuilt by the Maratha queen Ahilyabai Holkar after earlier destruction. A living temple.

primary.account: Damaged in the medieval Deccan campaigns and later rebuilt (finally by Ahilyabai Holkar).

sites.name: Badrinath Temple
sites.builder: Ancient; re-established by Adi Shankaracharya (8th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: A Vishnu temple at ~3,100 m in the Garhwal Himalaya — BOTH one of the four Char Dham AND part of the Chota Char Dham. Re-established by Adi Shankaracharya; open only in season.

sites.name: Dwarkadhish Temple (Jagat Mandir), Dwarka
sites.builder: Attributed to Vajranabha (Krishna's descendant); present temple ~16th c. on older foundations
sites.lifespan_note: Krishna's legendary city of Dwarka on the Gujarat coast — one of the four Char Dham. The 5-storey Jagat Mandir flies the world's largest temple flag, changed several times daily.

sites.name: Yamunotri Temple
sites.builder: Built by Maharani Gularia of Jaipur (19th c.); rebuilt after damage
sites.lifespan_note: The seat of the goddess Yamuna near the river's source at ~3,290 m — the first stop of the Chota Char Dham. Repeatedly damaged by Himalayan weather and rebuilt.

sites.name: Gangotri Temple
sites.builder: Built by the Gorkha general Amar Singh Thapa (18th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: The seat of the goddess Ganga near her source at ~3,415 m, in the Greater Himalaya — part of the Chota Char Dham. Open only in the pilgrimage season.

sites.name: Hinglaj Mata Temple (Nani Mandir), Balochistan
sites.deity: Hinglaj Mata (Shakti — a shapeless stone; a Shakti Peetha)
sites.builder: Ancient cave shrine in the Kirthar/Makran hills; one of the 51 Shakti Peethas
sites.lifespan_note: A cave shrine on the Hingol river in the Makran desert — one of the 51 Shakti Peethas and the largest Hindu pilgrimage in Pakistan (the Hinglaj Yatra draws ~250,000). Revered by local Muslims too, who call it 'Nani Mandir'. Living proof of a continuous Sanatan presence in Balochistan.

sites.name: Katas Raj Temples (Qila Katas), Chakwal
sites.deity: Shiva (and Rama, Hanuman) around a sacred pool
sites.builder: Hindu Shahi kings (~615–950 CE), around the sacred Katas pool
sites.lifespan_note: A complex of seven temples around a holy pool said in legend to have formed from Shiva's tears; linked to the Pandavas' exile (Dvaitavana). A major pilgrimage site abandoned at the 1947 Partition; partly restored, worship resumed for pilgrim groups.

primary.account: The Hindu community migrated to East Punjab in 1947 and the complex was abandoned; decades of neglect (and groundwater loss to nearby cement plants) damaged it. Not a deliberate demolition — a loss through displacement.

source.label: Punjab Archaeology Dept; World History Encyclopedia — Katas Raj

sites.name: Panchmukhi Hanuman Mandir, Karachi
sites.builder: Ancient shrine (~500 CE) in Soldier Bazaar
sites.lifespan_note: Believed ~1,500 years old — among the oldest temples in Karachi, protected under the Sindh Cultural Heritage Act 1994. Houses a naturally-formed five-faced Hanuman murti; 2019 expansion uncovered centuries-old deity statues. A living temple answering directly your point that Karachi's Hindu heritage is real and present.

source.label: Wikipedia — Panchmukhi Hanuman Temple; Arab News (2019 discovery)

sites.name: Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, Karachi
sites.builder: Swaminarayan Sampraday (completed 1788)
sites.lifespan_note: The only surviving Swaminarayan temple in Pakistan, on M. A. Jinnah Road. A refugee camp in 1947 (Jinnah himself visited); the Hinglaj Yatra still starts from here. An active temple at the heart of a Karachi Hindu neighbourhood.

sites.name: Multan Sun Temple & Prahladpuri Temple
sites.builder: Ancient — the Sun Temple noted in Greek accounts (~515 BCE); Prahladpuri linked to the Narasimha/Prahlada legend
sites.lifespan_note: Multan's celebrated Sun Temple was one of the most famous shrines of the ancient subcontinent, its wealth described by Arab and Greek writers. Destroyed after the Muslim conquest of Multan; the adjacent Prahladpuri temple was reduced over centuries and the last structure was lost in 1992.

primary.account: The Multan Sun Temple, hugely wealthy, was destroyed after the Muslim conquest; the Prahladpuri temple was damaged repeatedly and its final structure collapsed amid the 1992 communal violence.

source.label: Wikipedia — Prahladpuri Temple; Multan Sun Temple

sites.name: Amb Temples, Salt Range
sites.builder: Odi Shahi dynasty (9th–10th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: A 9th–10th c. Hindu temple complex on Sakesar peak — the westernmost of the Salt Range string that includes Katas Raj and Tilla Jogian. The 15 m 'Temple B' is the loftiest Odi Shahi temple. Abandoned ruin.

sites.name: Nagarparkar Jain Temples (incl. Gori Temple), Sindh
sites.builder: Śvetāmbara Jain community, Maru-Gurjara style (12th–15th c.; Gori Temple 1375)
sites.lifespan_note: A group of ~14 abandoned Śvetāmbara Jain temples in the Karoonjhar hills; the Gori Temple (1375) holds the oldest surviving Jain frescoes in the northern subcontinent. On the UNESCO tentative list — proof that Jain heritage, too, spanned what is now Pakistan.

source.label: Wikipedia — Nagarparkar Jain temples; Gori Temple

sites.name: Kalka Cave Temple, Aror (ancient capital of Sindh)
sites.historical_region: Aror / Roruka, capital of ancient Sindh, undivided India
sites.state: undivided India (present-day Pakistan, near Rohri, Sindh)
sites.builder: Rai dynasty (a great Shiva temple); cave shrine of Kalka Devi
sites.lifespan_note: At Aror (Roruka) — capital of the Sauvira kingdom and of Hindu Sindh under Raja Dahir until the Arab conquest (712 CE). A natural-cave Devi temple, among the holiest Hindu sites in Pakistan, still visited. Roruka is also named in early Buddhist literature — a genuinely multi-faith ancient city.

sites.name: Great Bath, Mohenjo-daro
sites.builder: Indus (Harappan) Civilisation — no named ruler; the script is undeciphered
sites.lifespan_note: The 'earliest public water tank of the ancient world' (c. 2500 BCE), 12×7 m and 2.4 m deep, watertight with bitumen — widely read as a ritual bathing structure, a possible root of later Dharmic purification practice. Mohenjo-daro (pop. ~40,000) was abandoned c. 1700 BCE. NOTE: attributing a religion to the Indus Valley is speculative — the script is undeciphered and there are no confirmed temples; this is included as a proto-historic SACRED/ritual site, honestly labelled.

source.label: UNESCO — Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro; Britannica — Great Bath

sites.name: Kalibangan Fire Altars
sites.builder: Indus (Harappan) Civilisation
sites.lifespan_note: On the dried Ghaggar-Hakra (identified by some with the Vedic Sarasvati), Kalibangan yielded rows of mud-brick 'fire altars' — among the few Harappan sites with them — argued to preforeshadow Vedic fire (yajna) ritual, and the earliest known ploughed field (c. 2800 BCE). The fire-altar interpretation is debated. ASI-excavated (B. B. Lal / B. K. Thapar).

sites.name: Dholavira (Harappan city)
sites.builder: Indus (Harappan) Civilisation
sites.lifespan_note: A great Harappan city in the Rann of Kutch, famed for its cascade of stone reservoirs, a large ceremonial ground, and the still-undeciphered 'Dholavira signboard'. UNESCO World Heritage (2021). Included as a proto-historic site whose religion is unknown, not as a temple.

source.label: ASI; UNESCO — Dholavira: a Harappan City

sites.name: Rakhigarhi (largest Harappan site in India)
sites.builder: Indus (Harappan) Civilisation
sites.lifespan_note: The largest Harappan settlement in the Indian subcontinent, on the Ghaggar-Hakra plain. Ancient-DNA work here (2019) informs the debate on the population ancestry of South Asia — relevant to the DNA/population-shift layer on the wishlist. ASI-documented since the 1960s; museum under construction.

source.label: ASI; Rakhigarhi ancient-DNA study (Shinde et al., 2019); Wikipedia

sites.name: Teotihuacan (Pyramid of the Sun)
sites.deity: Mesoamerican gods — the 'City of the Gods'
sites.builder: The Teotihuacano civilisation (unknown builders)
sites.lifespan_note: A vast pre-Aztec ceremonial metropolis; the Pyramid of the Sun is the third-largest pyramid on Earth. The Aztecs, arriving later, named it 'the place where the gods were created'. The original city collapsed ~650 CE.

sites.name: Templo Mayor, Tenochtitlan (Mexico City)
sites.builder: The Mexica (Aztec) empire
sites.lifespan_note: The great double pyramid at the heart of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan. Razed by the Spanish after 1521; a cathedral and colonial city were built directly over it. Rediscovered under Mexico City in 1978. The clearest case of a temple erased and overbuilt by a colonial-Christian power.

primary.account: After the fall of Tenochtitlan the temple was demolished and Mexico City's cathedral raised over the sacred precinct; the Mexica religion was suppressed.
primary.toll_note: The conquest of the Americas caused catastrophic indigenous death (war + disease); White's chart puts the toll at ~15 million.

source.label: UNESCO — Historic Centre of Mexico City; Wikipedia — Templo Mayor

sites.name: Chichén Itzá (Temple of Kukulcán)
sites.builder: The Maya (and Toltec-influenced) civilisation
sites.lifespan_note: A great Maya city whose step-pyramid (El Castillo) is aligned so that a serpent of light descends its stairway at the equinoxes. Abandoned before the Spanish arrived; a surviving monument of Maya astronomy-religion.

sites.name: Machu Picchu
sites.deity: Inca — Inti (Sun); the Intihuatana & Temple of the Sun
sites.builder: Inca emperor Pachacuti
sites.lifespan_note: A royal Inca estate and sacred site in the Andes, with the Temple of the Sun and the Intihuatana ritual stone. Uniquely, the Spanish never found it, so it escaped the destruction inflicted on other Inca shrines — which is why it survives so intact.

source.label: UNESCO — Historic Sanctuary of Machu Picchu

sites.name: Coricancha (Temple of the Sun), Cusco
sites.builder: The Inca Empire (its walls once sheathed in gold)
sites.lifespan_note: The most sacred temple of the Inca, its walls once covered in gold. After the conquest the Spanish stripped the gold and built the Santo Domingo convent directly on top of the Inca stonework — which still stands, and survived earthquakes that toppled the colonial church above it. A literal layering of colonial power over a native temple.

primary.account: The Inca sun temple was looted of its gold and a Dominican convent built over it; Inca religion was suppressed across the Andes.

sites.name: Tiwanaku (Kalasasaya & the Sun Gate)
sites.builder: The Tiwanaku civilisation
sites.lifespan_note: A monumental pre-Inca ceremonial centre near Lake Titicaca, with the Gateway of the Sun. One of the mother-cultures of the Andes, revered by the later Inca themselves.

sites.name: Cahokia (Monks Mound)
sites.builder: The Mississippian culture (Native American)
sites.lifespan_note: The largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico (~18,000 people), centred on Monks Mound — the biggest earthwork pyramid in the Americas. A Native American sacred/ceremonial capital, largely abandoned before European contact. UNESCO World Heritage.

source.label: UNESCO — Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site

sites.name: Chaco Canyon (Pueblo Bonito)
sites.builder: The Ancestral Puebloans (Chacoan culture)
sites.lifespan_note: A monumental Ancestral Puebloan ceremonial centre of astronomically-aligned great houses and kivas. Sacred to today's Pueblo, Hopi and Navajo peoples. UNESCO World Heritage — a Native American holy landscape, still living in memory.

sites.name: Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela
sites.builder: King Gebre Meskel Lalibela, Zagwe dynasty
sites.lifespan_note: Eleven churches carved top-down from solid rock in the 12th–13th c. to recreate Jerusalem in Ethiopia — the Church of St George (Bete Giyorgis) is the most famous. A living centre of Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity, one of the world's oldest churches. UNESCO World Heritage.

sites.name: Great Zimbabwe
sites.builder: Ancestors of the Shona people
sites.lifespan_note: The largest ancient stone city in sub-Saharan Africa, capital of a great kingdom, whose conical tower and enclosures had ritual significance. Colonial-era authorities long denied Africans built it — an erasure later overturned. The nation of Zimbabwe is named for it.

sites.name: Ile-Ife (Yoruba holy city)
sites.builder: The Yoruba people (kingdom of Ife)
sites.lifespan_note: The Yoruba holy city, believed to be where creation began and humankind was founded by Oduduwa; famed for its naturalistic bronze and terracotta heads. Still the spiritual centre of the Yoruba religion, which also survives across the African diaspora (Santería, Candomblé).

sites.name: Lalish — holiest temple of the Yazidis
sites.deity: Yazidism (Tawûsî Melek); tomb of Sheikh Adi ibn Musafir
sites.builder: The Yazidi people — an ancient pre-Abrahamic faith of the Kurdish region
sites.lifespan_note: The spiritual heart of Yazidism, a native faith with roots older than Islam that blends ancient Iranian/Mesopotamian and nature-worship elements. The Yazidis were subjected to genocide by ISIS in 2014 (Sinjar) — a living example of a native people crushed between larger religious powers. Included because they, too, deserve to exist on the map.

source.label: UNESCO tentative list — Lalish Temple; Wikipedia — Lalish

sites.name: Göbekli Tepe — the world's oldest temple
sites.builder: Pre-Pottery Neolithic hunter-gatherers
sites.lifespan_note: The oldest known temple on Earth — monumental T-shaped pillars raised by hunter-gatherers ~9600 BCE, 6,000 years before Stonehenge and 7,000 before the pyramids. It rewrote the story of religion: temples may have come BEFORE farming and cities. Only ~5% excavated. UNESCO World Heritage.

sites.name: Karnak Temple (Precinct of Amun-Ra), Thebes
sites.builder: Successive pharaohs over ~2,000 years (Middle Kingdom → Ptolemaic)
sites.lifespan_note: The largest religious building ever constructed — a vast complex to Amun-Ra at Thebes (Luxor), built and expanded across two millennia of pharaohs. The Hypostyle Hall's 134 giant columns remain. The heart of ancient Egyptian religion. UNESCO World Heritage.

source.label: UNESCO — Ancient Thebes with its Necropolis

sites.name: Great Ziggurat of Ur
sites.builder: King Ur-Nammu of the Third Dynasty of Ur (Sumer)
sites.lifespan_note: A massive stepped Sumerian temple-platform to the moon god Nanna, ~4,100 years old, in one of humanity's first cities. Among the oldest monumental religious structures on Earth; partly reconstructed.

sites.name: Parthenon, Acropolis of Athens
sites.builder: Athenian democracy (Pericles; architects Iktinos & Kallikrates)
sites.lifespan_note: The temple of Athena atop the Acropolis, the icon of classical Greece. Later a church, then a mosque; badly damaged in 1687 when a Venetian shell hit Ottoman gunpowder stored inside. A temple re-purposed by each ruling faith in turn.

sites.name: Delphi — Temple of Apollo & the Oracle
sites.builder: The Panhellenic sanctuary (ancient Greek city-states)
sites.lifespan_note: Considered by the Greeks the navel (omphalos) of the world; the Oracle here shaped decisions across the ancient Mediterranean. Closed in 393 CE when the Christian emperor Theodosius banned pagan cults.

primary.account: The oracle and sanctuary were shut down when Theodosius outlawed pagan worship across the empire — an early state suppression of a native faith by an Abrahamic one.

sites.name: Stonehenge
sites.deity: Unknown — Neolithic/Bronze Age ritual & solar alignment
sites.builder: Neolithic & Bronze Age peoples of Britain
sites.lifespan_note: The most famous prehistoric monument in Europe — a ring of standing stones aligned to the solstices, built and rebuilt over ~1,500 years. Its builders' religion is unknown; it remains a living sacred site for modern Druids and pagans. UNESCO World Heritage.

source.label: UNESCO — Stonehenge, Avebury and Associated Sites

sites.name: St Basil's Cathedral, Moscow
sites.builder: Tsar Ivan the Terrible (architects Barma & Postnik)
sites.lifespan_note: The iconic swirl of coloured onion domes on Red Square, built to mark the conquest of Kazan. A Russian Orthodox landmark; secularised as a museum under the USSR and preserved. UNESCO World Heritage (Kremlin & Red Square).

source.label: UNESCO — Kremlin and Red Square, Moscow

sites.name: Arkaim (Bronze-Age Sintashta site)
sites.builder: The Sintashta culture (early Indo-Iranian / Steppe pastoralists)
sites.lifespan_note: A fortified Bronze-Age settlement of the Sintashta culture — the same Steppe / Indo-Iranian world the ancient-DNA layer links to the Yamnaya ancestry that reached both Europe and India. Often read as a proto-Aryan ritual/astronomical site. A tangible tie between the Steppe and the subcontinent's deep history.

sites.name: Temple at Uppsala (Norse)
sites.builder: Norse/Germanic pagans (Gamla Uppsala cult centre)
sites.lifespan_note: The great pagan temple of Gamla Uppsala, described by Adam of Bremen as gold-adorned with idols of Thor, Odin and Freyr. Norse religion was suppressed as Sweden Christianised; the temple was destroyed/replaced by a church in the late 11th c. A royal burial-mound landscape survives.

primary.account: The pagan cult site was suppressed and a church built at Gamla Uppsala as Norse religion was replaced by Christianity.

sites.name: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) — the Moai & Ahu
sites.builder: The Rapa Nui (Polynesian) people
sites.lifespan_note: Nearly 1,000 monumental moai statues on ceremonial platforms (ahu) representing deified ancestors — one of the most remote and remarkable sacred landscapes on Earth. Missionary contact and disease in the 19th c. nearly ended the native religion. UNESCO World Heritage.

sites.name: Uluru (Ayers Rock) — Anangu sacred site
sites.builder: The Anangu (Pitjantjatjara & Yankunytjatjara) — sacred for tens of thousands of years
sites.lifespan_note: A giant sandstone monolith sacred to the Anangu, woven through their Tjukurpa (creation law) — among the world's oldest continuous sacred sites, holy for tens of thousands of years. Climbing was permanently banned in 2019 out of respect. A living Aboriginal holy place. UNESCO World Heritage.

sites.name: Fire Temple of Yazd (Atash Behram)
sites.builder: Zoroastrian community; sacred fire dated to ~470 CE (building 1934)
sites.lifespan_note: Enshrines a sacred fire burning since ~470 CE — the highest-grade Zoroastrian fire in Iran. Zoroastrianism, the ancient faith of pre-Islamic Persia, shaped ideas across many later religions; its followers are now a tiny, endangered minority in their homeland. A native faith that predates the Abrahamic religions.

sites.name: Iranshah Atash Behram, Udvada
sites.builder: The Parsi (Zoroastrian) community who fled Persia to India (~8th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: The oldest Zoroastrian sacred fire in India, brought by Parsis fleeing Islamic conquest of Persia; consecrated at Sanjan in 721 CE, now at Udvada. A powerful case of India sheltering a persecuted native faith — the Parsis found refuge here and endure. Their fire has burned for ~1,300 years.

sites.name: Niyamgiri (Niyam Dongar), sacred mountain of the Dongria Kondh
sites.deity: Niyam Raja (the King of Law) — the mountain itself is sacred
sites.builder: No building — a living sacred landscape of the Dongria Kondh people (~8,000–10,000)
sites.lifespan_note: The Dongria Kondh worship Niyam Raja, who is believed to dwell at Niyam Dongar, the Mountain of the Law. They call themselves Jharnia, 'protectors of the streams'. In 2013, in a Supreme-Court-mandated vote, all 12 village councils rejected Vedanta's bauxite mine — a rare victory for an indigenous people defending a sacred site against industry. Included because native sacred sites are usually erased, not mapped.

source.label: Survival International; Wikipedia — Niyamgiri; Sacred Land Project

sites.name: Mawphlang Sacred Grove (Law Kyntang)
sites.deity: Labasa — the guardian deity of the grove
sites.builder: Preserved by the Khasi people (Lyngdoh Mawphlang clan) for ~800+ years
sites.lifespan_note: The oldest and best-known Khasi sacred grove — a forest of 500+ species where taking even a leaf is taboo. A living, unbuilt 'temple' of Khasi indigenous religion, guarded by the deity Labasa. Sacred natural sites like this are Dharma of the land itself, older than any temple architecture.

source.label: Meghalaya Tourism; Sahapedia — Mawphlang Sacred Grove

sites.name: Sarna Sthal — sacred sal groves of the Adivasi (Sarnaism)
sites.deity: Sarna Maa / the village goddess, worshipped under the sal tree
sites.builder: Munda, Oraon, Santhal, Ho, Asur, Baiga and other Adivasi peoples
sites.lifespan_note: Sarnaism is the indigenous nature-religion of the Chhotanagpur plateau — worship under the sal tree in a sacred grove (sarna sthal), no idol, no building. Millions of Adivasis follow it; there is a long-standing demand for a separate 'Sarna' religion code in the Indian census. Marked as a tradition-wide entry (representative point at Ranchi), because it is a living faith of tens of millions that most maps simply omit.

source.label: Mongabay India — Protecting sarna; Wikipedia — Sarnaism / Jaherthan

sites.name: Khejarli — the Bishnoi tree-martyrs' grove
sites.builder: The Bishnoi community; memorial to Amrita Devi & 363 martyrs (1730)
sites.lifespan_note: In 1730, when the Maharaja of Jodhpur's men came to fell khejri trees, Amrita Devi and then 363 Bishnois were killed hugging the trees rather than let them fall — the earliest recorded environmental martyrdom, and the root of the later Chipko movement. A living tradition where protecting nature IS the religion.

source.label: Wikipedia — Khejarli; Global Nonviolent Action Database

sites.name: Bhimbetka Rock Shelters
sites.deity: Prehistoric rock art — no known deity
sites.builder: Palaeolithic-to-historic peoples of the Vindhya range
sites.lifespan_note: Over 750 rock shelters with India's oldest known art, some shelters inhabited 100,000+ years ago — the deepest layer of human presence on the subcontinent, before any named religion. UNESCO World Heritage. The true 'aboriginal' baseline the whole atlas rests on.

source.label: ASI; UNESCO — Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka

sites.name: Hire Benakal Megalithic Site
sites.builder: Iron Age / megalithic ('aboriginal') communities of the Deccan
sites.lifespan_note: One of India's largest prehistoric megalithic necropolises — hundreds of dolmens ('mora angadi') on a hill, pre-dating Vedic temple culture. On India's UNESCO tentative list. Represents the 'aboriginal' / pre-temple sacred landscape the user asked to include.

source.label: ASI; UNESCO tentative list — Hire Benakal

sites.name: Junapani Cup-Marked Megaliths
sites.builder: Iron Age megalithic communities (Vidarbha)
sites.lifespan_note: Stone circles near Nagpur with enigmatic cup-marks, some argued to have astronomical alignments — among the pre-Vedic sacred/funerary sites of central India.

sites.name: Kailasa Temple 'ancient machining' claim
sites.builder: Claim popularised by Praveen Mohan (independent YouTuber)
sites.lifespan_note: Praveen Mohan argues the smoothness of drill/tool marks at Kailasa implies lost high-powered machining technology and a far shorter build time.
sites.rebuttal: Not accepted by academic archaeology. Mainstream consensus (ASI, art historians) attributes the temple to Rashtrakuta artisans using iron chisels, hammerstones and a planned top-down excavation over decades; experimental estimates show a few hundred labourers could complete it in years, and tool marks throughout are consistent with hand-carving. No physical or textual evidence of machinery exists.

source.label: Praveen Mohan (YouTube) — claim; Wikipedia & LiveHistoryIndia — mainstream rebuttal

sites.name: Vettuvan Koil 'unfinished pyramid' claim
sites.builder: Documented: Pandya dynasty rock-cut temple (~8th c.); claim popularised by Praveen Mohan
sites.lifespan_note: A genuine Pandya-era monolithic rock-cut Shiva temple at Kalugumalai. Praveen Mohan and others describe it as a 'pyramid' with anomalous precision and speculate about advanced ancient technology.
sites.rebuttal: The monument is a well-documented, unfinished 8th-c. Pandya rock-cut temple carved top-down (like Kailasa). The 'pyramid / lost technology' framing is not supported by archaeologists, who read it as an incomplete conventional temple.

source.label: ASI (Pandya rock-cut temple); Praveen Mohan (contested framing)

sites.name: Elephanta Caves (Trimurti Shiva)
sites.builder: Kalachuri dynasty (King Krishnaraja), mid-6th c.
sites.lifespan_note: Rock-cut Shiva cave-temples on Gharapuri island off Mumbai; the 6 m three-headed Trimurti (Creator-Preserver-Destroyer) is a masterpiece of Indian art. Damaged by the Portuguese, who reportedly used the reliefs for target practice. UNESCO World Heritage. LiDAR + photogrammetry scanned by CyArk (2023).

primary.account: Portuguese occupiers are recorded damaging the sculptures (target practice); several panels are defaced.

sites.name: Petra — the Monastery (ed-Deir) & Treasury
sites.builder: The Nabataeans (peak under King Aretas IV)
sites.lifespan_note: The rose-red rock-cut city of the Nabataeans — temples and tombs carved into sandstone cliffs (Al-Khazneh the 'Treasury', ed-Deir the 'Monastery'). A caravan-trade capital of a native Arabian faith before Rome and Islam. UNESCO World Heritage; LiDAR-scanned by CyArk.

sites.name: Tikal (Temple of the Great Jaguar)
sites.builder: The Maya (Temple I built for king Jasaw Chan K'awiil I, ~732 CE)
sites.lifespan_note: One of the greatest Maya cities, its steep limestone temple-pyramids rising above the Petén jungle. Temple I (47 m) is a royal funerary pyramid. Abandoned ~10th c.; UNESCO World Heritage. CyArk-scanned.

sites.name: Chavín de Huántar
sites.builder: The Chavín culture
sites.lifespan_note: A major Andean pilgrimage and oracle centre ~900–200 BCE, with underground galleries housing the Lanzón — a fanged anthropomorphic deity. One of the mother-cultures of the Andes, long before the Inca. UNESCO World Heritage; CyArk-scanned.

sites.name: Great Mosque of Djenné
sites.builder: The people of Djenné (present structure 1907, on 13th-c. foundations)
sites.lifespan_note: The largest mud-brick building in the world, the icon of Sudano-Sahelian architecture. Re-plastered every year by the whole community in a festival (crépissage). Included as a distinctly African form. UNESCO World Heritage; CyArk-scanned.

source.label: UNESCO — Old Towns of Djenné; CyArk

sites.name: Bagan (temple plain)
sites.builder: Kings of the Pagan Kingdom
sites.lifespan_note: Over 2,000 surviving Buddhist temples and stupas on a plain by the Irrawaddy — the capital of the Pagan Kingdom and one of the greatest concentrations of Buddhist monuments on Earth. Damaged by the 2016 earthquake. UNESCO World Heritage; aerial-LiDAR scanned (CyArk / Open Heritage).

source.label: UNESCO — Bagan; CyArk / Open Heritage (aerial LiDAR)

sites.name: Preah Vihear Temple
sites.builder: Khmer Empire (esp. Suryavarman I & II, 11th–12th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: A cliff-top Shiva temple in the Dângrêk mountains, built along a rare 800 m north–south axis over four reigns. A UNESCO World Heritage site fought over by Cambodia and Thailand (an ICJ case). LiDAR-scanned by CyArk.

source.label: UNESCO — Temple of Preah Vihear; CyArk

sites.name: Lamanai (High Temple)
sites.builder: The Maya (occupied 3,000+ years)
sites.lifespan_note: One of the longest continuously-occupied Maya cities (over 3,000 years, right up to European contact), on the New River Lagoon. Famous for the Mask Temple and the High Temple. CyArk-scanned.

sites.name: Patan Durbar Square (Krishna Mandir)
sites.builder: Malla kings of Lalitpur (Newar architecture)
sites.lifespan_note: A royal square of tiered Newar temples (the stone Krishna Mandir, 1637) in Lalitpur — one of the three Durbar Squares of the Kathmandu Valley, where Hindu and Buddhist Newar traditions blend. Damaged in the 2015 earthquake; CyArk-scanned for restoration. UNESCO World Heritage.

sites.name: Amarbayasgalant Monastery
sites.builder: Built by the Manchu Qing emperor Yongzheng (1727–1737)
sites.lifespan_note: One of Mongolia's three great Buddhist monasteries, dedicated to Zanabazar (whose body was moved here). Rare among Mongolian monasteries in surviving the 1930s Stalinist religious purges. CyArk-scanned.

primary.account: Mongolia's 1930s purges destroyed most of its ~700 monasteries and killed thousands of monks; Amarbayasgalant was among the few partly spared.

sites.name: Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove
sites.builder: The Yoruba people (living grove; shrines by artist Susanne Wenger, 20th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: One of the last primary high forests in southern Nigeria — the sacred grove of the Yoruba goddess Osun, dense with shrines and sculptures. A living centre of the Yoruba religion (which also survives across the African diaspora). CyArk-scanned. UNESCO World Heritage.

sites.name: El-Kurru (Nubian pyramids of Kush)
sites.builder: Kings of Kush (the 25th 'Nubian' Dynasty — Piye, Shabaka, Tanwetamani)
sites.lifespan_note: A royal cemetery of steep Nubian pyramids of the Kushite kings who ruled Egypt as the 25th Dynasty — Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt. CyArk-scanned the Tomb of Tanwetamani. Part of the Napatan region UNESCO listing.

source.label: UNESCO — Gebel Barkal & Napatan region; CyArk

sites.name: Mosque City of Bagerhat (Sixty Dome Mosque)
sites.builder: Khan Jahan Ali, Bengal Sultanate (15th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: A lost 15th-century city of 360 brick mosques and monuments (the Sixty Dome Mosque is the largest) in the Bengal delta. CyArk-scanned. UNESCO World Heritage.

source.label: UNESCO — Historic Mosque City of Bagerhat; CyArk

sites.name: Lukang Longshan Temple
sites.builder: Qing-dynasty Hokkien settlers (moved to present site 18th c.)
sites.lifespan_note: The best-preserved Qing-dynasty building in Taiwan, a Guanyin temple famed for its woodcarving. Damaged in the 1999 earthquake and restored — CyArk-scanned as part of the recovery.
